pages.title: Introduction to time complexity
pages.content:
Time complexity is a way to measure how long an algorithm takes to run as the amount of **input data** increases. Think of it as a method for figuring out how **fast or slow** an algorithm is.

There are multiple ways to measure time complexity of an algorithm:
1. Best case
2. Average case
3. Worst case

We will focus on understanding the **worst-case scenario** of how an algorithm performs. We use a special notation called “Big O notation” to talk about worst-case time complexity.

#### Why is Time Complexity important?
Time complexity of an algorithm is independent from the machine the algorithm is going to run on. Understanding time complexity is important because it gives us a way of **comparing algorithms** without worrying about the system on which the algorithms are going to run.

pages.title: Finding time complexity - Rule 1
pages.content:
To find out time complexity of an algorithm, we look at the number of operations performed based on the input size.

Let's take a look at the below code:
```python
a = 1
b = 2
print(a + b)
```

In the above algorithm, there is no input. In total three operations are being performed in three lines. Every single operation is denoted as O(1) (pronounced as Big O of 1).

Thus, for the above example, we have time complexity as `O(1) + O(1) + O(1) = 3 * O(1)`

But we denote the time complexity of the above algorithm as O(1), ignoring the constant 3.

#### Rule 1 - Ignore the constants
When calculating time complexity, we ignore the constant values because they don’t matter when the input size becomes large.

Thus O(1), 5 * O(1), 8 * O(1) are all O(1)

### Task
What will be the time complexity of this algorithm?

```python
a = 4
print(a)
```

pages.title: Finding time complexity - O(N)
pages.content:
Let's look at another algorithm now.
```python
for i = 0 to N
    print(i)
```

In the above algorithm, we are running a loop from 0 to N. In total the loop will run **N** times. For each iteration of the loop we are doing one operation `print(i).

The final time complexity will be: N * O(1) => O(N).

This time the algorithm dependent on a variable N and with that the time complexity also has the value N.

### Task

What if we were doing two operations inside the loop?
```python
for i = 0 to N
    print(i)
    print(i * 2)
```

callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Finding time complexity - O(N) and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Finding time complexity - Rule 2
pages.content:
Let's see a different example now.

```python
a = 4 + 5
for i = 0 to N
    print(a)
```

Can you determine the time complexity of this algorithm?

Time complexity of first line => O(1)
Time complexity of the loop => O(N)

Total time complexity => O(1) + O(N).

But can we use two Big Os to define time complexity of an algorithm?
Nope

#### Rule 2 - Focus only on the largest factor
If an algorithm has multiple different parts with different time complexity, when determining the final time complexity we only look at the largest factor.

Because the biggest factor will slow down an algorithm the most.

Thus the time complexity of the above algorithm will be: **O(N)**

### Task
Can you determine final time complexity of the given algorithm, considering the two rules?
```python
for i = 0 to N
    print(i)

for j = 0 to N
    print(j)
```

callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Finding time complexity - Rule 2 and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Finding time complexity - Nested loops
pages.content:
Let's take a bit complex algorithm now.
```python
for i = 0 to N
    for j = 0 to N
        print(i)
        print(j)
```

What do you think will the time complexity be?

This is a nested loop. The outer loop runs N times. And for each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop also runs N times.

For each iterations of inner loop there are two operations.

Complexity of line 3 and 4 => O(1) + O(1) => **O(1)**

Total complexity of inner loop => N * (complexity of line 3 and 4) => N * O(1) => **O(N)**

Total complexity of outer loop => N * (complexity of line 2 - 4) => N * O(N) => **O(N * N)**

It can also be represented as **O(N ^ 2)**

Notice how the number of operations are multiplied in case of nested codes.

### Task
Now can you find the complexity of this algorithm?
```python
for i = 0 to N
    for j = 0 to N
        for k = 0 to N
            print(i)
```

pages.title: Summary of Time Complexity
pages.content:
In this lesson we learned all about Time complexity.

Time complexity is a way to measure how long an algorithm takes to run as the amount of **input data** increases.

We learned about how to find time complexity by counting the number of operations performed in an algorithm.

We also learned about two rules of finding time complexity of an algorithm
1. Ignore constants
2. Focus only on the largest factor

We ignore constants when finding the final time complexity. Also, if there are multiple pieces of an algorithm with varying time complexity, we only take the largest factor.

We also learned how to calculate time complexity of nested loops.

In the next lesson we will see how we have to break the Rule 2 sometimes and also how to apply time complexity to DSA problems in general. 

Then we will practice a lot of problems on finding time complexity.

pages.title: Two loops
pages.content:
We have learned about the basic algorithms and their time complexities in the last few lessons, but there are many different algorithms and thus there can be a lot of different variations in time complexity as well.

See this algorithm:
```python
for i = 0 to N
    print(i)

for j = 0 to M
    print(j)
```

What do you think will the time complexity be? Let's calculate.

First loop => O(N)  
Second loop => O(M)

Total => **O(N + M)**

But Rule 2 says that we only care about the largest factor no?

We cannot ignore either of N or M because both are variable and we don't know which one is bigger or smaller. So we have to keep both of them in the final complexity.

If we are already given that M is very large as compared to N, then we can say the complexity is O(M). But in general case, it is still **O(N + M)**.

### Task
Now can you think of what the time complexity will be for this algorithm?
```python
for i = 0 to N
    print(i)

for j = 0 to M
    print(j)

for i = 0 to N
    print(i)
```

pages.title: Time complexity for DSA
pages.content:
We will solve a lot of examples on time complexity, but let’s take a break and think about the applications of time complexity when it comes to solving DSA problems.

Remember how each problem statement on SEED-IT has a **Constraints** section. This section talks about the constraint on the size of input given to you.

The constraints section generally look like this:  
$1 \leq N \leq 10^5$

This means that the value of N can range from 1 to 10^5.

----

For harder problems it is not enough that your solution is correct, it also has to be efficient enough to run within the given time limit.

In general, you can assume that the current day computers can run up to 10 ^ 8 operations per second. You can calculate the worst case time complexity of your algorithm and check if the total number of operations are beyond 10 ^ 8. If the operations performed by your algorithm exceeds 10 ^ 8, you will get TLE or Time limit exceeded.

### Task
What will the number of operations performed by your algorithm be, if maximum value of N can be 10 ^ 6 and time complexity of the algorithm is O(N)?

pages.title: Time complexity of standard algorithms
pages.content:
Hope you have got an idea on how to figure out whether your algorithm will work or give TLE based on the constraints provided.

The steps are - 
1. Find the worst case time complexity of your algorithm
2. Put the maximum possible value of N according to the constraints and check the approximate number of operations
3. If the operations are below $10 ^ 8$, your algorithm can run otherwise it will give TLE.

---

Let's now look at time complexity of some of the standard algorithms. Remembering this numbers help you quickly decide whether you can do that operation or not based on the constraints.

### Loops
| Algorithm | Complexity | Max value of N possible | 
|---------- |----------|----------|
| Single loop till N | $O(N)$ | $10 ^ 8$ |
| Nested loops both till N | $O(N ^ 2)$ | $10 ^ 4$ |
| Two loops one by one till N | $O(N)$ | $10 ^ 8$ |


### Searching
| Algorithm | Complexity | Max value of N possible | 
|---------- |----------|----------|
| Linear search | $O(N)$ | $10 ^ 8$ |
| Binary search | $O(log N)$ | $10 ^ {10 ^ 8}$ |


### Sorting
| Algorithm | Complexity | Max value of N possible | 
|---------- |----------|----------|
| Bubble sort, insertion sort | $O(N ^ 2)$ | $10 ^ 4$ |
| Merge sort | $O(N log N)$ | $10 ^ 7$ |


### Array or list operations
| Algorithm | Complexity |
|---------- |----------|
| Adding an element at the end of a list | $O(1)$ |
| Adding an element at the start of a list | $O(N)$ |
| Counting the occurrences of a number in an array | $O(N)$ |

pages.title: Log N time complexity
pages.content:
Till now we have seen time complexity of loops which run linearly from 1 to N, thus having approximately N number of operations. Even if we are incrementing $i$ by 1, 2 or 10, the constant doesn't really matter.

But there are certain types of loops which do very few operations than N and thus we need other ways to denote their time complexity.

Look at the below code for an example
```python
i = 1
while i <= n:
    print(i)
    i *= 2
```

Here $i$ is getting doubled in each iteration.

For $n = 4$, the iterations will be
```python
1
2
4
```
Only 3 iterations. 

How about $n = 16$?
```python
1
2
4
8
16
```
Only 5 iterations.

**Can we calculate the total number of iterations for any $n$?**  
In each iteration, $i$ is getting doubled, so the values of $i$ will be
$1, 2, 4, 8, \ldots, n$.

If we can count the total number of values of $i$, we will know the time complexity. This is because time complexity is nothing but a measure of the number of operations in an algorithm.

**Now, how do we calculate the total number of iterations?**  
If you observe, all the values of $i$ are of the form $2^x$.  
$2^0, 2^1, 2^2, 2^3, \ldots, 2^x$

The last value will be less than or equal to $n$.

In the above series, we can see, in total, there are $x + 1$ values. Thus, we can say, that there were $x + 1$ iterations of the loop.

**How do we find $x$ then?**  

We know that $2^x \leq n$  

Taking the logarithm on both sides.

$\log_2(2^x) \leq \log_2(n)$  

$\log_2(2^x) \equiv xlog_2(2)$   
$\log_2(2)$ is $1$.

Thus, the equation becomes:  
$x \leq \log_2(n)$

The maximum possible value for $x$ is $\log_2(n)$, and $x$ denotes the maximum number of times the loop will run. Thus, the time complexity of this algorithm will be $\log_2(n)$, as figured out by the total number of operations done in the loop.

----

In general, you can remember that anytime a variable in loop is multiplied by a number greater than 1, the time complexity of the loop will be of the form: $log(n)$.

pages.title: Square root N time complexity
pages.content:
Now that we have learned about $log(N)$ time complexity, there is only one other non-linear time complexity which is important to know: $O(sqrt(N))$.

That is the number of operations of an algorithm is approximately $sqrt(N)$.

This is an example of a code with $O(sqrt(n))$ time complexity.
```python
i = 1
while i * i <= n:
    print(i)
    i += 1
```

In this, even though $i$ is incremented by 1 in each iteration, the value of $i$ has to go only till $i * i <= n$.


#### How do we calculate the total number of times the loop is running?
It's simple. The iterations will be: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, \ldots, x$, until $(x *x) \leq n$.

**Let's solve for $x$:**

Given the condition $x^2 \leq n$, we aim to find the value of $x$ that satisfies this inequality.

1. **Initial inequality:**  
   $x^2 \leq n$

2. **Taking the square root on both sides:**  
   $\sqrt{x^2} \leq \sqrt{n}$

3. **Simplifying:**  
   $x \leq \sqrt{n}$

Thus, the maximum possible value of $x$ can be $\sqrt{n}$, making it the time complexity of the given algorithm.

### Task
What is the complexity of this algorithm?
```python

   j = 0
   while j * j <= n:
      print(i + j)
      j = j + 1
```

pages.title: Harmonic series
pages.content:
Let's look at another interesting example:
```python
for i = 1 to n
    j = 0
    while j < n:
        j += i 
        print(i + j)
```

To analyze the time complexity of the given code, let's break it down into its two main parts: the outer loop and the inner while loop.

1. **Outer loop**: This loop runs from 1 to $n$, so it iterates $n$ times.

2. **Inner while loop**: The behavior of this loop depends on the value of $i$ from the outer loop. For each iteration of the outer loop, $j$ starts at 0 and increases by $i$ until it reaches or exceeds $n$. This means the number of iterations of the inner loop for each value of $i$ is approximately $\frac{n}{i}$.

To find the total time complexity, we sum the number of iterations of the inner loop over all iterations of the outer loop:

$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{n}{i}
$

$\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{i}$ is the harmonic series which grows logarithmically. Thus, the sum can be approximated as $n \log n$.

Therefore, the time complexity of the given code is $O(n \log n)$.

pages.title: Introduction to Space complexity
pages.content:
Space complexity refers to the amount of **memory or space** an algorithm requires to run as a function of the **input data size**. Alongside time complexity, it is an important aspect of analyzing an algorithm's efficiency.

#### Key Points:

**Space Complexity = Auxiliary Space + Input Space:** This means we consider both the extra memory needed by the algorithm and the memory required for the input data.

**Memory Usage:** This includes the memory for variables, data structures, and function calls.

**Auxiliary Space:** This is the extra memory the algorithm uses, excluding the input data. We mainly focus on this because the input size is usually fixed.

**Big O Notation:** We use this to describe the worst-case space usage of an algorithm.

#### Why It Matters?

Understanding space complexity helps prevent memory issues and ensures that algorithms work efficiently, especially when dealing with large data or limited resources.

pages.title: Finding space complexity
pages.content:
To determine an algorithm's space complexity, we examine the amount of extra memory used based on the input size.

Let's take a look at the following code:
```cpp
int a = 1
int b = 2
cout << a + b;
```
The above algorithm declares two variables *a* and *b*. Each variable takes constant space, which is independent of the input size. Every single variable takes **O(1)** space.

Thus, for the above example, we have the space complexity as:

**O(1) + O(1) = 2 * O(1)**

However, we denote the above algorithm's space complexity as **O(1)**, ignoring the constant 2.

**Ignore the constants**
When calculating space complexity, we ignore the constant values because they don’t matter when the input size becomes large.

**Examine the code below:**
```cpp
cout << "Hello";
```

pages.title: Understanding Space Complexity of Algorithms
pages.content:
When analyzing space complexity, we focus on the amount of memory that an algorithm or data structure requires about the size of the input. The space can be categorized into **input space** (the space taken up by the input data) and **auxiliary space** (the extra memory used by the algorithm for computation).

#### Space Complexity of Common Algorithms
|  *Algorithms*   | *Auxiliary Space* | *Input Space* |
| -------------   | -------------     | -----------   |
| Linear Search   |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Binary Search   |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Selection Sort  |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Bubble Sort     |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Insertion Sort  |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Merge Sort      |      O(n)         |    O(n)       |
| Quick Sort      |      O(log n)     |    O(n)       |
| Radix Sort      |      O(n+k)       |    O(n)       |
| Counting Sort   |      O(n+m)       |    O(n)       |
| Heap Sort       |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Bucket Sort     |      O(n)         |    O(n)       |

- Quicksort has a space complexity of O(log(n)) in the average case. It can be O(n) due to an unbalanced partitioning leading to a deep recursion stack in the worst case.
- k is the range of input in Radix sort.
- Counting Sort requires O(N+M), where N and M are the space taken by outputArray[] and countArray[] respectively.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Understanding Space Complexity of Algorithms and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Trade-Off
pages.content:
#### The trade-off between space and time complexity:
It is basically a problem-solving technique in which we solve a problem :
- Either in less time and using more space, or
- In very little space by spending more time.

The trade-offs between time and space complexity are often *inversely proportional*, meaning that improving one may worsen the other.

The best algorithm is the one that helps to solve a problem that requires less space in memory as well as takes less time to generate the output. But in general, it is not always possible to achieve both of these conditions at the same time.

If a problem is slow but memory-efficient, using more memory can speed it up. Conversely, if a solution is fast but memory-intensive, using less memory might slow it down.

**Example:**  
- Selection sort uses o(n^2) time complexity but no auxiliary space. Space complexity o(1)
- But merge sort uses o(n log n) time complexity and extra O(n) space.

pages.title: Basic Concepts
pages.content:
**Definition of a Matrix**
   - A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. It's denoted by a capital letter, such as A, and its elements are represented by a subscript, where the first index denotes the row and the second index denotes the column. 

For example:


![mat](https://i.ibb.co/3CS4V35/matrix3x3.png)

**A** is a `3 x 3` matrix. Element $a_{23}$ is in second row and third column.
   
**Basic Properties and Terminology**
   - **Rows, Columns, and Elements**: A matrix consists of rows and columns, where each row represents a horizontal arrangement of elements, and each column represents a vertical arrangement of elements. The individual elements of a matrix are the numbers located at the intersection of a specific row and column.
   - **Types of Matrices (based on dimension)**:
     - *Square* Matrix: A matrix with an equal number of rows and columns, i.e., `M x M`.
     - *Rectangular* Matrix: A matrix with different numbers of rows and columns, i.e., `M x N`
 

**Representation of Matrices**
   - **Using 2D Arrays**: In programming languages like Python, C++, and Java, matrices are often represented using 2D arrays. Each element in the 2D array corresponds to an element in the matrix, with the first index representing the row and the second index representing the column.

pages.title: Matrix Types and Applications
pages.content:
### Other types of matrices:

Apart from the *square* and *rectangular* matrices, there are few other important categories of matrices. 

Some of which are listed below:

- **Identity Matrix:** An identity matrix is a special diagonal matrix where all diagonal elements are 1, and all non-diagonal elements are 0.

![Identmat](https://i.ibb.co/g6fC9YR/Identity-Mat.png)

- **Symmetric Matrix:** A symmetric matrix is a square matrix that is equal to its transpose.The entries of a symmetric matrix are symmetric with respect to the main diagonal.
  *Note:* The transpose of a matrix is found by interchanging its rows into columns or columns into rows

![symmat](https://i.ibb.co/Ch8pD57/symmetric-Mat.png)

- **Sparse Matrix:** A sparse matrix is a matrix in which most of the elements are zero. Sparse matrices are often used in situations where storage space needs to be optimized.

![sparsemat](https://i.ibb.co/Jyd3nSZ/sparse-Mat.png)


### Some of the real-life applications of matrix data structure are:

- **Image Processing and Computer Graphics**: Matrices represent digital images and enable operations like manipulation and rendering.

- **Geographic Information Systems (GIS)**: Matrices handle spatial data for tasks such as mapping and terrain analysis.

- **Machine Learning and Data Analysis**: Matrices organize datasets for tasks like classification and regression in machine learning.

- **Network Analysis and Social Networks**: Matrices model connections in networks for analysis and prediction.

- **Finance and Economics**: Matrices aid in financial modeling, risk analysis, and economic forecasting.

pages.title: Steps for Merging Two Sorted Arrays
pages.content:
Given two sorted arrays:

$A= [a1, a2, ..., an]$

$B= [b1, b2, ..., bm]$

- **Initialize Pointers:**

$i = 0, j = 0, k = 0$

$i$ for Array A

$j$ for Array B

$k$ for the new Array C.

- **Compare and Merge:**

While both arrays have elements:
Compare $A[i]$ and $B[j]$.
Place the smaller element into $C[k]$.
Increment i or j (whichever had the smaller element) and k.

- **Copy Remaining Elements:**

If Array $A$ has remaining elements, copy them to $C$.
If Array $B$ has remaining elements, copy them to $C$.

### Example
**Given:**

$A = [1, 3, 5]$

$B = [2, 4, 6]$

**Steps:**

- Compare $1$ and $2$, place $1$ into $C$.

- Compare $3$ and $2$, place $2$ into $C$.

- Compare $3$ and $4$, place $3$ into $C$.

- Compare $5$ and $4$, place $4$ into $C$.

- Compare $5$ and $6$, place $5$ into $C$.

- Copy remaining element $6$ from Array $B$ to $C$.

### Result:

$C: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]$

This efficiently merges the two sorted arrays into one sorted array.

pages.title: Pseudocode of merge sort
pages.content:
```cpp
function MERGE-SORT(A, left, right)
    if left < right
        middle = (left + right) / 2
        MERGE-SORT(A, left, middle)
        MERGE-SORT(A, middle + 1, right)
        MERGE(A, left, middle, right)

function MERGE(A, left, middle, right)
    // // Merge the subarrays A[left..middle] and A[middle+1..right] into a single sorted subarray.   
```

### Explanation:
- **MERGE-SORT(A, left, right):** Recursively divides the array into two halves until each subarray contains a single element. Then, calls the MERGE function to merge the sorted subarrays.

- **MERGE(A, left, middle, right):** Merges two sorted subarrays into a single sorted subarray.
n1 and n2 represent the lengths of the left and right subarrays.
Copies the elements of the left and right subarrays into temporary arrays L and R.
Merges the elements back into the original array A in sorted order.

## Task
- Given two arrays of length 3:
- $Array 1$ = [10, 26, 2]
- $Array 2$ = [94, 55, 93]
- Your task is to merge these two arrays into a single array of length 6 in such a way that the merged array is lexicographically smallest. When merging, you must maintain the relative positions of the elements within each of the original arrays.

pages.title: Quick Sort - Pseudo Code
pages.content:
```
function quicksort(arr, low, high):
    if low < high:
        pi = partition(arr, low, high)
        quicksort(arr, low, pi - 1)
        quicksort(arr, pi + 1, high)

function partition(arr, low, high):
    pivot = arr[high]
    i = low - 1
    for j = low to high - 1:
        if arr[j] < pivot:
            i = i + 1
            swap arr[i] with arr[j]
    swap arr[i + 1] with arr[high]
    return (i + 1)

```

### Quick Sort Function (`quicksort`)
**Purpose**: Recursively sorts the array.

**Steps**:
- If the array has more than one element (low < high):
- Partition the array and get the pivot index (pi).
- Recursively sort the sub-arrays before and after the pivot.

### Partition Function (`partition`)
**Purpose**: Rearranges the array so that elements less than the pivot are on the left and elements greater than the pivot are on the right. Places the pivot in its correct position.

## Task
- Given the following array and pivot element, **perform the partitioning step of the Quick Sort** algorithm and choose the correct configuration of the array after partitioning around the pivot.

- $Array: [9, 3, 8, 4, 7, 2, 6, 1, 5]$

- **$Pivot$** : 5

pages.title: Pseudo Code
pages.content:
```cpp
function countingSort(array):
    if array is empty:
        return
    
    maxValue = findMaxValue(array)
    minValue = findMinValue(array)
    range = maxValue - minValue + 1

    // Create and initialize the counting array
    count = array of size range initialized to 0
    output = array of the same size as input

    // Count occurrences of each element
    for each element num in array:
        index = num - minValue
        count[index] = count[index] + 1

    // Accumulate counts
    for i from 1 to range - 1:
        count[i] = count[i] + count[i - 1]

    // Build the output array
    for i from length(array) - 1 down to 0:
        num = array[i]
        index = num - minValue
        output[count[index] - 1] = num
        count[index] = count[index] - 1

    // Copy the output array to the original array
    for i from 0 to length(array) - 1:
        array[i] = output[i]
```
### Key Points
- **Time Complexity**:  Counting sort has a time complexity of O(n+k), where n is the number of elements in the input array, and k is the range of the input values.
- **Space Complexity**: The space complexity is O(n+k) because it requires additional space for the counting array and output array.
- **Stability**: Counting sort is stable, meaning it preserves the relative order of equal elements, 
- **Limitations**: Counting sort is most effective when the range of the input values is not significantly larger than the number of elements. For large ranges, the counting array can become impractically large.

Counting sort is best suited for scenarios where the range of possible values is limited and known ahead of time. 

## Task:
- Given the following unsorted array:
- $Array = [4,2,2,8,3,3,1]$
- What is the correct accumulated count array after performing the counting sort process?

pages.title: Radix Sort
pages.content:
Radix sort is a sorting algorithm that organizes numbers or strings by processing each digit or character, starting from the least significant one and moving to the most significant one. It distributes items into buckets based on their current digit or character, collects them back, and repeats the process for each digit or character position until all are sorted.

### How Radix Sort Works
- **Identify the Maximum Value**: Determine the maximum value in the dataset to know the number of digits or characters to process.

- **Sort by Each Digit**:Least Significant Digit (LSD) First: Start with the least significant digit (the rightmost digit). Distribute the elements into buckets based on this digit.
Sort Each Bucket: After distributing elements into buckets, collect them back in order. This ensures elements are sorted by the least significant digit.

- **Move to the Next Digit**: Move to the next more significant digit (moving left). Repeat the bucket distribution and collection process for this digit.

- **Repeat Until Sorted**: Continue this process for each digit or character until you reach the most significant digit (the leftmost one).

- **Final Collection**: After processing all digits, the collection of elements will be sorted.

pages.title: What is linear search
pages.content:
**Linear search**, also known as sequential search, is a simple searching algorithm that checks each element in a list one by one until the desired element is found or the list ends.

### **Real-Life Example:**

Imagine you have piles of papers on your desk, and you're looking for a specific document. Here's how a linear search would work in this scenario:

- You pick up the first paper on the pile and check if it's the document you need.
- If it is the document you need, you stop searching because you've found it.
- If it's not the document, you put it aside and pick up the next paper in the pile.
- You repeat this process, checking each paper one by one, until you find the document or reach the end of the pile.

pages.title: Stability and Inplace Sorting algorithm
pages.content:
A sorting algorithm is stable if it maintains the relative order of equal elements. For example, if two elements have the same value, their order remains the same as in the input array.

**Example:**

- Input: [(4, 'apple'), (2, 'banana'), (4, 'pear')]
- Stable Sort Result (sorted by the left element): [(2, 'banana'), (4, 'apple'), (4, 'pear')]
- Unstable Sort Result (sorted by the left element): [(2, 'banana'), (4, 'pear'), (4, 'apple')]
- Stable sorting is important when multiple criteria are involved, and the order of equal elements matters.

### In-Place Sorting
An in-place sorting algorithm uses a constant amount of extra space for producing the final sorted array. The sorting is done within the original array with only a small, constant amount of extra storage.

**Example**

- Quick Sort: Uses a divide-and-conquer approach but sorts elements within the array.
- Insertion Sort: Inserts elements into their correct position within the array without needing extra space.

pages.title: Bubble Sort Algorithm Analysis
pages.content:
### Time Complexity
- **Worst Case:** O(n2)(when the list is sorted in reverse order)
- **Best Case:** O(n)(when the list is already sorted)
- **Average-case:** O(n2)

### Space Complexity
- Bubble sort is an in-place sorting algorithm, so it requires 𝑂(1) additional space.

### Characteristics
- **Stability:** Bubble sort is a stable sorting algorithm, meaning that it maintains the relative order of items with equal keys.
- **Adaptive:** While not adaptive by default, it can be made adaptive by adding a flag to detect if any swaps were made in a pass. If no swaps were made, the algorithm can terminate early.

topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Insertion Sort.

pages.title: Pseudocode of Insertion Sort
pages.content:
```cpp
for i = 1 to length(A) - 1
    key = A[i]
    j = i - 1
    while j >= 0 and A[j] > key
        A[j + 1] = A[j]
        j = j - 1
    A[j + 1] = key

```
### Example
Consider the following array: [5, 2, 4, 6]
- Start with the first element: [5 | 2, 4, 6]
- Take the next element (2) and insert it into the sorted part: [2, 5 | 4, 6]
- Take the next element (4) and insert it: [2, 4, 5 | 6]
- Take the next element (6) and insert it: [2, 4, 5, 6]

### Time Complexity
- Best Case: O(n) – The array is already sorted.
- Average Case: O(n2)
- Worst Case: O(n 2) – The array is sorted in reverse order.
### Space Complexity
- O(1) – Only a constant amount of extra space is needed.

pages.title: Time Complexity Analysis of Binary Search
pages.content:
### Analysis of Worst Case Complexity

In the worst case of the algorithm we would be finding the element in the last iteration of the Binary Search Algorithm and at each step of the iteration, the size of the array reduces to half so there can be at max of total of $log_2{N}$ iterations hence the Worst Case Complexity of the algorithm is $O(log_2{N})$.

In case the above reasoning wasn't clear to you, think of it this way:

Let $2^k$ be the first power of $2$ which is $\ge N$. Now, if we do a binary search on an array of size $2^k$, after the first step, the 'solution space' would be $\frac{2^k}{2} = 2^{k-1}$. Similarly, after the second step, it would be $\frac{2^{k-1}}{2} = 2^{k-2}$, and so on. So clearly, within $k$ steps, we reach a size of $2^0 = 1$, which is our termination case. So we spend $O(k)$ time. And $k$ is nothing but $ceil(log_2{N})$, which is at most $log_2{N}+1$, which is $O(log_2{N})$. 

We can show that the average case complexity is also $O(log_2{N})$.

pages.title: Binary Search on arbitrary Predicate
pages.content:
This variation is used when we have a boolean search space, meaning we have to find the optimal solution where a certain condition is true. 

We can visualize the search space as a boolean array.  
For us to use Binary search to find an optimal solution the boolean array must be sorted, meaning all the true values must be on one side and all the false values on the other side. 

Let's say we have a problem and want a value that solves our problem but we want the most optimal solution, meaning we want to find the smallest value that solves our problem. 

Assume we have a function that returns true if the value solves our problem and false if the value does not solve our problem. 

In this case, our search space will look like this. 
```
[False, False, False,  ....., False, True, True, True, ..., True]
    0       1      2            x-1     x   x+2   x+3          N
```
Here the value $X$ is the first value that will solve our problem.   
So, We can either go through all these values until we get to $x$ which will cost us $O(N)$ time or we can use Binary Search to find $x$ which can find the value in $O(log_2N)$ time.

We can take $left$ as the lowest possible solution and $right$ as the highest possible solution and in each iteration, we cut our search space in half. 
- If the middle value gives **False** then the solution is on the right, i.e., we set $left$ = $middle + 1$. 
- If the middle value gives **True** then the solution can be on the left, i.e., we set $right = middle$.
- We repeat this until the search space contains only one value which satisfies the solution.

pages.title: Multiple Choice Question
pages.content:
For $r$ rows, we know that the number of coins needed is $1 + 2 + ... + r = r(r+1)/2$.

Let us call f(r) = $r(r+1)/2$.

So, if we have an infinite array whose elements are f(1), f(2), ..... , then we know that

- This array is increasing
- The answer is the last index such that f(r) = n. So we only need till n.

Also, we can use an implicit array, because we can find f(r) very quickly. So instead of having an array, we'll just have a function which returns f(r).

Now, how do we find the last index such that f(r) <= n?

pages.title: Linked List - Operations
pages.content:
The primary operations which we do on a linked list are:
- **Insertion**: Inserting an element at end/beginning or in the middle at some k-th position.
- **Deletion**: Deleting an element from the list.
- **Display**: Traversing the whole linked list and output each element.

Because linked list is a basic data structure, you can do many more operations on it as required. But these three are enough to start.

Let's learn about each of these in the coming lessons.

pages.title: Introduction - Doubly Linked List
pages.content:
Doubly linked list, an extension of singly linked list allows us to store not only a next pointer, but also a previous pointer. Therefore, every node points to its next and previous node.    

This provides us benefits like traversing back and forth but the trade-off is extra space. We need to maintain an extra pointer for every node.       

The structure of the node now is:

 - Datatype value
 - node next
 - node prev

Note - The prev pointer of head is null and the next pointer of the tail is null.    

Some applications of Doubly Linked List are:     

 1) Implementing LRU (Least Recently Used) cache algorithm
 2) Used in applications where undo redo use-cases are applicable
 3) Deletion operation in O(1) time using map.

modules.description: This module covers the fundamental concepts of stacks, including push, pop, peek, and isEmpty operations. It also teaches stack implementation using arrays and libraries, and includes practice problems on valid parentheses, expression evaluation, and finding next greater/smaller elements.

topics.title: How to implement a Stack
topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for How to implement a Stack.

pages.title: Stack Introduction
pages.content:
A stack data structure is a collection that follows a specific order in which operations are performed. The order is Last In, First Out (LIFO). This means that the last element added to the stack will be the first one to be removed.

To visualize a stack, consider a pile of books placed one on top of the other. Here's how the stack data structure would work in this analogy:

**Adding a book (Push operation):**
When you add a new book to the stack, you place it on top of the existing pile. This is similar to the "push" operation in a stack data structure. You can only add (push) a new book at the top of the pile, not in the middle or at the bottom.

**Removing a book (Pop operation):**
When you want to remove a book from the stack, you always take it from the top. This is like the "pop" operation. You can't remove a book from the middle or the bottom without first removing all the books on top of it. Popping a book off the stack reveals the book that was previously underneath it, which you can then read or pop off next.

**Peeking at the top book (Peek operation):**
If you want to check which book is currently at the top of the stack without removing it, you can take a quick look. In stack terminology, this is called a "peek" operation, where you're inspecting the element at the top of the stack without modifying the stack itself.

**Checking if the stack is empty:**
If you've removed all the books from the pile and there are none left, your stack of books is now empty. In the stack data structure, you can perform an operation to check whether the stack is empty before attempting to pop, which would be an error since there's nothing to remove.

**Size of the stack:**
The number of books in the pile at any given time corresponds with the size of the stack. As you add (push) and remove (pop) books, the size of your stack changes.

In the stack of books analogy, it's clear that you have access only to the topmost book and don't have direct access to the books lower down in the pile. Similarly, in a stack data structure, you generally only have access to the top element, reflecting the LIFO principle. This makes the stack an ideal structure for certain applications, such as undo mechanisms in software, function call stacks in programming languages, and parsing expressions in compilers.

pages.title: Use cases of Stack
pages.content:
Stacks are used whenever you need to manage a collection of items that follows the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) order of processing. \
This means that the last element added to the collection is the first one to be removed. \
Stacks are commonly used in various programming scenarios, including:
- **Expression Evaluation:** Stacks are widely used in evaluating expressions, particularly mathematical expressions. \
For example, they can be used to convert infix expressions (e.g., 3 + 4 * 2) to postfix (or reverse Polish notation) expressions for easy evaluation.
- **Function Calls and Recursion:** The call stack in C (and many other programming languages) is implemented as a stack. \
When a function is called, its return address and local variables are pushed onto the call stack.\
As functions return, their data is popped off the stack.
- **Undo/Redo Functionality:** Stacks can be used to implement undo and redo functionality in applications, allowing users to revert changes they've made and redo them.
- **Backtracking Algorithms:** Stacks are commonly used in algorithms that require backtracking, such as depth-first search, where you need to store a history of choices made to explore different paths.
- **Parsing and Syntax Analysis:** Stacks can be used during parsing to check whether parentheses, brackets, and other symbols are balanced and properly nested.

----

In this lesson, we covered
1. What is Stack?
2. Different operations which can be performed on a stack
3. How to implement stack using Array / List.

In the next lesson, we learn how to use the standard inbuilt Stack library which is already available in most languages. Then we will move on to solving real world problems using Stack.

pages.title: Different ways of implementing stacks
pages.content:
In many languages, there are multiple methods you can use to implement stacks.

- **Using an Array:** \
Implementing a stack using an array is straightforward. \
You define an array to hold the elements and a variable to keep track of the top of the stack. \
The primary advantage of this method is that it's memory-efficient since you allocate memory only for the elements you need. \
However, the downside is that the stack size is fixed and can't easily be resized without creating a new array.
- **Using a Linked List:** \
You can also use a singly linked list to implement a stack. \
In this approach, you treat the head of the linked list as the top of the stack. \
Linked lists offer dynamic sizing and are more memory-efficient than arrays when the stack size changes frequently. \
However, linked lists have more overhead due to the pointers.
- **Using inbuilt libraries:** \
The Standard Template Library in C++, or inbuilt libraries of Python provides multiple in-built classes including stack. The implementation details are hidden from you and methods like push, top, pop, etc., are available for the functionality. We will learn more about this in later sections.

pages.title: Queues - implementation
pages.content:
Let's explain queues with a simple real-world example involving people waiting in line at a bus stop.
- **Introduction to the Queue / The Queue Setup:**\
Queue is a data structure that follows the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principle, where the first person (or item) to arrive is the first one to be served or processed - just like in a bus line
- **Enqueuing (Adding to the Queue):**\
People join the queue when they arrive at the bus stop. \
They stand at the end of the line and wait for the bus.
- **Dequeuing (Removing from the Queue):**\
When the bus arrives, the driver opens the door and allows passengers to board in the order they arrived (FIFO).
- **Peeking at the Front Passenger:**\
The driver may want to know who the next passenger is without letting them board yet.
- **Checking If the Queue Is Empty:**\
After the bus departs, the queue may become empty as all passengers have boarded.\
This is useful to determine if more passengers are waiting or if the service (the bus in this case) can close.

### Task

- Given a empty queue, q1.
- Perform the following operation over q1.
- Push(or Enqueue) 5, Push 6, Push 7, Pop (or Dequeue).

**Note left side will be the head of the queue**

pages.content:
What will be the remaining deque after performing the following operations?

Here, we will use 
- push_front(x) - to push x in the front of deque
- push_back(x) -  to push x in the back of deque
- pop_back() - to pop the last element of deque
- pop_front() - to pop the front element of deque


Initially you are given an empty deque.
### Operations
- push_front(5)
- push_back(6)
- push_back(3)
- push_front(5)
- push_front(9)
- pop_back()

***Note the left side will be the front of deque and the right side will be the back of deque***

modules.description: Learn about hashing, where data is mapped to hash values using a hash function. Also, explore how collisions occur when different inputs produce the same hash value and how to handle them using techniques like chaining and open addressing.

topics.title: What is Hashing?
topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for What is Hashing?.

pages.title: Hashing
pages.content:
Hashing transforms input data into a fixed-size value or key, typically using a mathematical function, for easier and more efficient storage, retrieval, and operations. This technique is commonly used in data structures like hash tables, where it helps to quickly locate and access data. The main goal of hashing is to optimize performance by minimizing the time required to search or retrieve stored values.

#### Need for Hashing
- Storing data in an array takes O(1) time, but searching in it takes at least O(log n) time. While this seems small, it can become inefficient with large datasets. 
- To solve this, hashing was introduced. The hash data structure allows both storing and retrieving data in constant time, O(1), making it much faster and more efficient for large datasets.

#### Applications of Hashing
- **Data Structures** - Hashing is used in various data structures for efficient operations on data.
- **Data Verifications** - Hashing is used to check if a file has been changed or tampered with.
- **Cryptography** - Hashing is used to encrypt sensitive data to keep it safe.
- **File Comparison** - Hash values of files can be used to compare files quickly.

pages.title: How Does Hashing Work
pages.content:
Hashing primarily involves three main components:


![image](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/hashing/hashing.png)

1. **Key:** The key can be a string, integer, or any immutable data type that serves as input to the hash function. It must be immutable (i.e., it cannot be modified after being created) to ensure that the hash value remains consistent. Common examples of immutable keys include strings, integers, and tuples.

2. **Hash Function:** The hash function takes the key as input and calculates an index within an array called a hash table. This index is referred to as the hash index. Some well-known hashing functions include MD5, SHA, and CRC. However, these functions are quite complex and fall outside the scope of this discussion.

3. **Hash Table:** The hash table is a data structure that uses a hash function to map keys to their corresponding values. It stores data in an associative way, where each value has a unique index within an array. 



Suppose we have a set of city names: `{"Delhi", "Paris", "London"}`. We want to store these names in a hash table efficiently.

There are several ways to do this; one approach is:

To simplify things, let's convert each character in the city name to its alphabetical position:
   - 'a' = 1, 'b' = 2, ..., 'z' = 26
   - We'll sum the alphabetical positions of all characters in the city name and use a table size of $10$. Our hash function will be `sum(string) % 10`.


Let's break down each city name into its alphabetical values:
   - For "Delhi":
     - 'D' = 4, 'e' = 5, 'l' = 12, 'h' = 8, 'i' = 9
     - Sum = 4 + 5 + 12 + 8 + 9 = 38
   - For "Paris":
     - 'P' = 16, 'a' = 1, 'r' = 18, 'i' = 9, 's' = 19
     - Sum = 16 + 1 + 18 + 9 + 19 = 63
   - For "London":
     - 'L' = 12, 'o' = 15, 'n' = 14, 'd' = 4, 'o' = 15, 'n' = 14
     - Sum = 12 + 15 + 14 + 4 + 15 + 14 = 74

Determine the Index in the Table Using Modulus Operation(our hash function).\
   The table size is 10, so we use the modulus operation to find the index for each city name:
   - For "Delhi":
     - Hash value = 38 % 10 = 8
     - Store "Delhi" at index 8 in the table.
   - For "Paris":
     - Hash value = 63 % 10 = 3
     - Store "Paris" at index 3 in the table.
   - For "London":
     - Hash value = 74 % 10 = 4
     - Store "London" at index 4 in the table.

Final Table Layout:

![image](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/hashing/hashing_example1.png)



This simple example helps illustrate the concept of hashing and how it efficiently maps strings to specific table indices for quick data access.

pages.title: Using Hashing to Optimize counting frequency
pages.content:
In the previous problem, to calculate the frequencies of elements in array A, a basic approach is to iterate over the array and count occurrences of each element, which takes **O(N^2)** time. However, we can optimize this using hashing.

Optimized Approach Using Hashing:
- Find the maximum value in $A$. This will determine the size of the $Hash$ array.
- Declare a $Hash$ array of size **max(A) + 1**, and initialize all elements to $0$.
- Iterate through $A$ and for each element $A_i$, increment the corresponding index in the Hash array.

Example:
For the array A = [1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 1, 2]:
Maximum value: 3
$Hash$ array of size 4: [0, 0, 0, 0]
After iterating through $A$:
```
index    0  1  2  3
        [0, 0, 0, 0]
1 ->    [0, 1, 0, 0]
2 ->    [0, 1, 1, 0]
2 ->    [0, 1, 2, 0]
2 ->    [0, 1, 3, 0]
3 ->    [0, 1, 3, 1]
1 ->    [0, 2, 3, 1]
2 ->    [0, 2, 4, 1]
```

Now, the Hash array represents the frequencies of elements in $A$.

This approach has a time complexity of **O(N + max(A))**, which is significantly more efficient than **O(N^2)**.

pages.title: Use Hashing
pages.content:
You might've implemented something like - 
- Fix an index $j$ in a loop.
- For each element at index $j$, you fix another index $i$ in the prefix $A[1...j−1]$.
- Now, count the number of indices $i$ where $A[i]=A[j]^2$, meaning that the value at $A_i$ should be equal to the square of the value at $A_j$.

#### Steps:
- Initialize a Hash array: This array will store the frequency of elements in the prefix $A[1...j−1]$.
- Update the Hash array: As you iterate through the array, for each $j$, you:
    - Count how many times $A[j]^2$ has appeared in the prefix by checking its frequency in the Hash array.
    - Update the Hash array by incrementing the frequency of $A_j$.

Now, update $Hash$ according to the following pseudo-code.
```cpp
for j from 1 to N:
    Hash[A[j]] += 1
```

To count the number of beautiful pairs where current element is $j$, simply add the count of times its square has come till now.
```cpp
for j from 1 to N:
    ans += Hash[A[j] * A[j]]
    Hash[A[j]] += 1
```

pages.title: Conclusion
pages.content:
When we use hashing, we are trading time for memory. This means we can make our code faster by using more memory.

In the first example:
The input values range from $1$ to $10^4$.
Since this range is small, we can easily create a hash array and solve the problem.
Now, imagine if the input values were as large as $1$ to $10^9$. This approach would fail because creating an array large enough to store all possible values (from $1$ to $10^9$) would use too much memory.

However, there’s something important to notice:

The number of distinct values in the array is always smaller than or equal to the size of the array.
If the array has **N** elements, there will be at most N distinct values.
#### Thought-Provoking Question:
How can we handle values as large as 10^9 with just an array of size **N** (around $10^5$)?

topics.title: Hash collision and Hashmaps
topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Hash collision and Hashmaps.

pages.title: Collision
pages.content:
In the previous module, we learned how the hashing works. 

Let’s go through the same example again. Suppose we have the hash table with the cities `{"Delhi", "Paris", "London"}`.

![Image](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/hashing/hashing_example1.png)

And now we want to add `"Moscow"`.

We use the same hash function as before: convert each character in the city name to its alphabetical position, sum these values, and use `sum(string) % 10` to find the index.

Let's break down `"Moscow"` using alphabetical positions:
   - 'M' = 13, 'o' = 15, 's' = 19, 'c' = 3, 'o' = 15, 'w' = 23
   - Sum = 13 + 15 + 19 + 3 + 15 + 23 = 88
   - Hence for `"Moscow"`:
     - Hash value = 88 % 10 = 8


We need to store `"Moscow"` at index 8. However, index 8 is already occupied by **"Delhi"**. Such scenarios, when two different inputs produce the same hash value in hashing is called a **collision**.

![image](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/hashing/hash_collision.png)



#### Why Do Collisions Happen?

- **Fixed Table Size:** Hash tables have a fixed size, so the number of possible hash values is limited. When many keys are being hashed, the chance of two different keys mapping to the same index increases.
- **Hash Function Limitations:** Even a well-designed hash function will sometimes produce the same index for different keys because it processes the input into a limited range of values.

pages.title: Resolving Collisions
pages.content:
Hash collisions are inevitable when different keys produce the same hash value and map to the same index in a hash table. Proper collision handling is essential to maintain the efficiency of hash tables for quick insertion, deletion, and lookup operations. 


Here are the most common techniques used to handle collisions:

### Chaining

- **How It Works:**  
  In chaining, each index in the hash table points to a linked list (or another data structure, like an array or a tree) that contains all the elements that hash to the same index.
- **Steps:**
  1. If a collision occurs, the new element is added to the linked list at the index where the collision happened.
  2. During searches, the hash index is located, and the linked list at that index is traversed to find the desired key.
- **Pros:**  
  - Simple to implement.
  - Handles an unlimited number of collisions by dynamically growing the linked list.
- **Cons:**  
  - Could lead to inefficient search times if many elements are added to the same index (a long linked list).
  - Requires extra memory to store pointers in the linked list.

#### Example:
If both `"Delhi"` and `"Moscow"` hash to index 8, chaining will store them as a list at index 8:

![image](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/hashing/chaining.png)

pages.title: More Collision Resolution Techniques
pages.content:
### Open Addressing

In open addressing, all elements are stored within the hash table itself. When a collision occurs, the algorithm searches for another open slot using a specified probing method. Here are the main types of open addressing:

#### a. **Linear Probing**

- **How It Works:**  
  When a collision occurs, the algorithm checks the next available slot (in a linear sequence) until an empty one is found.
- **Steps:**
  1. Calculate the hash index.
  2. If occupied, move to the next index (index + 1) until an empty slot is found.
- **Pros:**  
  - Simple to implement.
- **Cons:**  
  - Can lead to **clustering**, where a group of occupied slots builds up, increasing the time for insertion and search.

**Example:**
If `"Delhi"` and `"Moscow"` hash to the same index (8), `"Delhi"` is stored at 8, and `"Moscow"` would be placed in the next available slot, 9.

![image](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/hashing/linear_probing.png)

#### b. **Quadratic Probing**

- **How It Works:**  
  Similar to linear probing, but instead of checking the next slot in a linear sequence, it probes using a quadratic function (e.g., $i$2 where $i$ is the number of attempts).
- **Steps:**
  1. Calculate the hash index.
  2. If occupied, move to `index` + 12, `index` + 22, `index` + 32, etc., until an empty slot is found.
- **Pros:**  
  - Reduces clustering compared to linear probing.
- **Cons:**  
  - Could still lead to secondary clustering.
  - More complex probing sequence than linear probing.


In addition to these methods, other hash collision resolution techniques include Double Hashing, Rehashing, and Separate Chaining with Balanced Trees.

pages.title: Introduction to Heaps
pages.content:
### Heaps
Heap is a data structure that is used to store elements in a structured way such that the top element always has the highest priority. Heap resembles a binary tree where each node has a higher priority than it's children.  
### Types of Heaps 
- **Min Heaps** - Here every element is smaller than or equal to it's children.
- **Max Heaps** - Here every element is greater than or equal to it's children. 
### Example  
  
The above image represents a max-heap, where each node is greater than it's children
- First node is 100 which is greater than its children nodes 19 and 36.
- Second node is 19 which is greater than its children nodes 17 and 3.
- Third node is 36 which is greater than its children nodes 25 and 1.
- Fourth node is 17 which is greater than its children nodes 2 and 7.
- Fifth node is 3 which has no children.
- Sixth node is 25 which has no children.
- Seventh node is 1 which has no children.
- Eighth node is 2 which has no children.
- Nineth node is 7 which has no children.  
Thus the property is satisfied for each node.
### Applications of Heaps
Some Common Applications of Heaps include: 
- **Greedy Algorithms** - Heaps are used in many greedy algorithms where we have to make the most optimal choice at every step. Since the top of the heap always has the highest priority, we can choose the top element at every step.
- **Scheduling Algorithms** - Heaps are very useful in algorithms where we have to schedule tasks based on their priority.
- **Sorting** - Heaps can be very useful in sorting elements based on priority.

pages.title: Representation of binary trees as array
pages.content:
To represent a binary tree as an array we store all the nodes level wise in the array.  
For Example - The binary tree
```
       2
     /   \
    4     7
  /  \   /  \
  8  15 10  18
 /
21
```
can be represented in array as **[2, 4, 7, 8, 15, 10, 18, 21]**  
Here the children of a node at index $i$ are stored at indexes $2i+1$ and $2i+2$.\
Note that the arrays is 0-indexed.

Root is index 0. The children of root will be $2 * 0 + 1 => 1$ and $2 * 0 + 2 => 2$.

pages.title: Time Complexity of Heap operations
pages.content:
In a binary heap, both insertion and deletion operations have a time complexity of $O(log N)$, where $N$ is the number of elements in the heap.  
### Insertion 
- In insertion we insert an element and swap with children if the property of heap is not satisfied.
- In worst case the element has the lowest priority and is moved to the depth of the binary tree.
- The depth of a binary tree is $log_{2}{N}$
### Deletion
- In deletion we swap the element to be deleted with the last element and pop the last element.
- We check all the children of the index which is deleted and if the Heap property is violated swap the elements and recursively check for the child.
- Similar to insertion in Worst case we may need to swap all the way to entire depth of the binary tree which is $log_{2}{N}$.
## Space Complexity
The n elements are stored in an array of size n. Thus the space complexity is $O(N)$, where $N$ is the number of elements in the heap.

pages.title: Basic Concepts
pages.content:
### Graph:
- Graphs are versatile data structures used to model relationships between entities. They consist of nodes (vertices) and edges. Graphs can be directed (edges have a specific direction) or undirected (edges have no direction). Graphs can also be weighted (edges have associated values) or unweighted.

![graph](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/graphs-ds.jpg)
### Node (or Vertex):
- Nodes are used to depict individual entities or points in the context of the problem being modeled by the graph. Nodes can carry additional information, such as labels or attributes, depending on the application. In social networks, nodes might represent individuals, while in a road network, nodes might represent intersections.

![Node](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/graphs-nodes.png)

### Edge:
- Edges represent relationships or connections between the entities represented by nodes. In an undirected graph, an edge is a two-way connection, whereas in a directed graph, edges have a specific direction from one node to another. Edges can also have weights, indicating the strength or cost of the connection. For example, in a transportation network, edges might represent roads, and the weight could represent the travel distance or time between two locations.

![edge](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/graph-edges.png)

pages.title: Graph Types - Undirected and Directed
pages.content:
#### Undirected Graph(or Bidirectional Graph):
- An undirected graph is a graph in which edges have no direction. The relationships between nodes are symmetric, meaning that if there is an edge connecting node A to node B, there is also an edge connecting node B to node A. 

Example: \
![graph](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/undirected-graph-with-7-nodes-and-7-edges.png)
### Key Characteristics:

- **Symmetry:** Edges do not have a specific direction, indicating a mutual relationship between connected nodes.
- **Edge Uniqueness:** There is typically only one edge between any pair of nodes, regardless of the order in which the nodes are listed.
- **Example Scenario:**
Consider a social network where nodes represent individuals, and edges represent friendships. In an undirected graph, the friendship is mutual, and the graph captures the symmetric nature of friendships.

### Directed Graph (Digraph/Unidirectional Graph):
- A directed graph, or digraph, is a graph in which edges have a specific direction. Each edge points from one node to another, indicating a one-way relationship.

Example: \
![graph](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/directed-graph-no-background.png)
#### Key Characteristics:

- **Directionality:** Edges have a clear direction, representing an ordered pair of nodes, where the edge starts from one node and points to another.
- **Asymmetry:** Unlike undirected graphs, directed graphs can have edges in only one direction between nodes or have edges in both directions.
- **Example Scenario:**
Consider a website where nodes represent web pages, and edges represent hyperlinks. In a directed graph, the hyperlinks direct traffic from one page to another, capturing the one-way flow of information on the internet.

pages.title: Connected, Disconnected and Weighted Graphs
pages.content:
### **Connected Graph:**

A connected graph is a graph in which there exists a path between every pair of nodes. In other words, every node is reachable from every other node by following the edges of the graph.

Example: 

![graph](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/connected-graph2.png)

**Key Characteristics:**
1. **Path Existence:** A path exists between any two nodes in the graph.
2. **Single Connected Component:** There is a single connected component, and no isolated nodes or subgraphs.

**Example Scenario:**
Imagine a transportation network where nodes represent cities, and edges represent roads. A connected graph ensures that there is a route between any two cities, facilitating seamless travel.

### **Disconnected Graph:**

A disconnected graph is a graph in which there are at least two nodes without a path connecting them. It consists of two or more connected components, each of which is a connected subgraph.

Example: 

![graph](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/disconnected-graph.png)


**Key Characteristics:**
1. **Isolated Nodes:** Nodes may exist without a path to reach other nodes in the graph.
2. **Multiple Connected Components:** The graph is comprised of two or more connected subgraphs.

**Example Scenario:**
Consider a social network where nodes represent individuals, and edges represent friendships. A disconnected graph may indicate the presence of isolated groups of friends with no connections between them.

### **Weighted Graph:**

A weighted graph is a graph in which each edge has an associated numerical value or weight. These weights can represent distances, costs, time, or any other relevant measure.

Example: 

![graph](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/weighted-graph.png)


**Key Characteristics:**
1. **Edge Weights:** Each edge is assigned a numerical value, indicating the significance or cost of the connection.
2. **Quantification of Relationships:** Weights provide a quantitative measure of the relationship between connected nodes.

**Example Scenario:**
In a communication network where nodes represent routers and edges represent communication links, a weighted graph can represent the latency or bandwidth associated with each link, allowing for optimization of data transfer.

pages.title: Trees and Forests
pages.content:
In graph theory, trees and forests are specialized structures that arise from the arrangement of nodes and edges in a graph. Understanding these concepts is fundamental for modeling hierarchical relationships and detecting cycles within a graph.

### **Tree:**

A tree in graph theory is an undirected graph with the following properties:

1. **Connected:** All nodes are connected by edges, and there is a unique path between any pair of nodes.
2. **Acyclic:** There are no cycles or closed loops in the graph.

Example:

![tree](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/tree-data-structure.jpg)


**Key Characteristics:**
1. **Root Node:** A designated node from which all other nodes are reachable. It has no incoming edges.
2. **Parent and Child Nodes:** Nodes in a tree are organized into parent-child relationships, forming a hierarchical structure.
3. **Leaves:** Nodes with no children in the tree are called leaves.

**Example Scenario:**
Consider a family tree, where each node represents an individual, and edges represent parent-child relationships. The resulting structure is a tree with a clear hierarchy and no cycles.

### **Forest:**

A forest is a collection of disjoint trees or, in other words, a graph without cycles. It can consist of one or more trees.

Example:

![forest](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/forest-tree-terminology.png) 


**Key Characteristics:**
1. **Disjoint Trees:** Trees in a forest do not share any common nodes or edges.
2. **Components:** Each tree in the forest is a connected component, and the entire forest may have multiple connected components.

**Example Scenario:**
In a computer network, nodes represent computers, and edges represent network connections. The absence of cycles ensures that there are no redundant or looping paths, creating a forest of disjoint trees.

pages.title: Graph Representations
pages.content:
Graphs, as fundamental structures in computer science and mathematics, can be represented in various ways to suit different applications. Three common representations are the Adjacency Matrix, Adjacency List, and Edge List. Let's explore each of these methods.

### **1. Adjacency Matrix:**

**Definition:** An adjacency matrix is a 2D array where the entry `matrix[i][j]` represents the presence or absence of an edge between nodes `i` and `j`.

**Explanation:**
- **Size:** The matrix is of size `N x N`, where `N` is the number of nodes in the graph.
- **Symmetry:** For an undirected graph, the matrix is symmetric since the relationship between nodes `i` and `j` is the same as between `j` and `i`.
- **Values:** If there is an edge between nodes `i` and `j`, `matrix[i][j]` (and `matrix[j][i]` in the case of an undirected graph) is set to 1; otherwise, it is 0.
  
**Example:**
Consider a graph with nodes A, B, and C. If there is an edge between A and B, `matrix[A][B]` and `matrix[B][A]` would be 1.

### **2. Adjacency List:**

**Definition:** An adjacency list is a collection of linked lists or arrays, where each node `i` has a list of its neighboring nodes.

**Explanation:**
- **Size:** The list contains `N` elements, one for each node in the graph.
- **Nodes and Neighbors:** Each element represents a node, and the associated list contains its neighboring nodes.
- **Flexibility:** Suitable for sparse graphs, as it doesn't require space for non-existent edges.

**Example:**
For the same graph, the adjacency list for node A might be [B, C] if there are edges connecting A to B and A to C.


### **Comparison:**

- **Adjacency Matrix vs. Adjacency List:**
  - Use an adjacency matrix for dense graphs with many edges.
  - Use an adjacency list for sparse graphs to save memory.

**Choosing the Right Representation:**
- **Adjacency Matrix:** Quick edge presence check, suitable for dense graphs.
- **Adjacency List:** Efficient for sparse graphs and efficient memory usage.

pages.title: Graphs Traversal Algorithms
pages.content:
### **Graph Traversal Algorithms**

**1. Breadth-First Search (BFS):**

**Concept:**
Breadth-First Search (BFS) is a graph traversal algorithm that systematically explores a graph by visiting all the nodes at the current depth before moving on to nodes at the next depth.


**Applications:**
- Finding the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
- Detecting connected components in a graph.

**2. Depth-First Search (DFS):**

**Concept:**
Depth-First Search (DFS) is a graph traversal algorithm that explores a graph by going as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking.

**Applications:**
- Topological sorting of directed acyclic graphs.
- Detecting cycles in a graph.

**Comparison:**

| `Criteria` | `Breadth-First Search (BFS)` | `Depth-First Search (DFS)` |
|----------|---------------------------|-------------------------|
| **Order**    | Level by level            | Depth by depth          |
| **Data Structure** | Queue               | Recursion or Stack      |
| **Path**     | Shortest path in an unweighted graph | Not necessarily the shortest path |
| **Memory**   | More memory intensive     | Less memory intensive   |



We'll learn more about each of these algorithms, in upcoming sections.

pages.title: Analysis of DFS
pages.content:
### **Time Complexity:**
- The time complexity of DFS is O(V + E), where V is the number of vertices (nodes) and E is the number of edges in the graph.
- Each vertex and edge is visited once in the worst-case scenario.

### **Space Complexity:**
- The space complexity of DFS is O(V) for the recursive implementation and O(V + E) for the iterative implementation using a stack.
- The space required is proportional to the maximum depth of the recursion stack or the maximum size of the stack.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Analysis of DFS and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Analysis of BFS
pages.content:
Each vertex takes $O(1)$ time to visit and to explore all $M$ edges we take $O(M)$ total time. \
So, the time complexity becomes $O(1 \cdot N + M)$, $O(N + M)$. \
Where $N$ is the number of vertices in the graph.

Since the queue size will be equal to the number of vertices at maximum, the space complexity is $O(N)$.

pages.title: What is Connected Component
pages.content:
In a graph, a connected component is a set of vertices (nodes) where each vertex is connected to every other vertex in the set, directly or indirectly, through edges (connections). In simpler terms, it's a group of vertices that are all somehow reachable from one another within the graph. Connected components are useful for understanding the structure and connectivity of a graph, helping to identify groups of related nodes.

For example, in the given graph we have 3 connected components:

pages.title: Cycles in Graphs
pages.content:
In graphs, a cycle is a series of edges that form a closed loop, where you can start and end at the same vertex by following the edges. In other words, you can travel through the graph, moving from one vertex to another along the edges, and eventually return to the starting vertex.

**Key points about cycles in graphs:**

1. **Closed Loop:** A cycle forms a closed loop, meaning there is no repetition of vertices (except for the starting and ending vertex) as you traverse the edges.

2 **Importance:** Cycles are significant in graph theory, and the presence or absence of cycles in a graph can determine its properties. Graphs without cycles are called acyclic, while those with at least one cycle are cyclic.

3. **Directed vs. Undirected Graphs:** Cycles can exist in both directed and undirected graphs. In a directed graph, the edges have a direction, and the cycle must follow the specified direction. In an undirected graph, the edges do not have a direction, and you can traverse them in either direction to form a cycle.

**Example:**
Consider the following undirected graph. We've a cycle with nodes `6`, `7` and `8` (6-7-8-6)

![ccbigraph](https://i.ibb.co/xgK9vTp/cycle-undirected-graph.png)

Similarly, in the following directed graph, we have a cycle with nodes `B`, `C`, `E` and `D` (B-C-E-D-B)

![ccunigraph](https://i.ibb.co/SXfpYfL/cycle-directed-graph.png)

pages.title: Example Use Of DSU
pages.content:
Suppose there is a network of friends in a social networking site and you wanted to check if two people are connected. 



You would typically traverse the whole network containing person 1 to check if person 2 is present on the same network.\
This task can be done more efficiently without traversing the whole network with the help of a data structure called Disjoint Set Union or DSU.\
Tasks like finding connected components, finding minimum spanning tree, identifying connected components in images and checking if two components are connected in networks like social networks and computer networks can be done very efficiently using DSU.  

In this course you'll learn all you need to know about DSU.

pages.title: Introduction to Disjoint Set Union
pages.content:
### Disjoint Set Union  
**Disjoint Set Union** or **DSU** is a data structure used to represents a group of unique elements as part of different sets. These sets are represented by a leader element.  
**For Example**  
Assume we have 8 nodes: **0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7**  
At first they all belong to individual sets.  
```
{0}     {1}      {2}      {3}       {4}        {5}          {6}        {7}
```
If we add a connection or an edge between 1 and 3 then the sets become
```
{0}   {12->1<-3}      {5}          {6}        {7}   
```
Now there are 5 sets and the second set is identified by the leader 1.

We store a set in the form of trees with the root of the tree being the leader of the set.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Introduction to Disjoint Set Union and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Need of DSU
pages.content:
DSU is very useful when dealing with data containing elements connected with one another. 
Some common uses of DSU include:  
- Keeping track of connected components in a graph
- Detecting cycles in a graph 
- Identifying mutual friends
- Calculating the minimum spanning tree in a graph
- Checking connected components in a computer network or social network

**For example**  
   
In this graph, we have seven components. A, B, C, and D would have the same leader in a DSU and thus would be in the same set. Similarly, G and F would have the same leader and thus would be in the same set. And E will be in another set. Thus making it very easy to find connected components in a graph.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Need of DSU and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Functions in DSU
pages.content:
There are two main operations in DSU:  
- **Find** - used to find the representative or leader of the set to which the element belongs
- **Union** - used to combine two sets

These are the only two functions a DSU provides, but they can be used to solve a wide variety of problems.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Functions in DSU and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Find in DSU
pages.content:
To store the elements in a DSU, we maintain an array called **parent**. The **parent** array holds the value of parent element for each element. If the element has no parent, it is saved as its own parent. At the beginning, when the graph has no edges or connections every element is its own parent.

The below set of elements will be represented like this in the parent array:  
0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3  
4  
5

Parent array => [1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5]

The parent of 0 is 1, 1 is 2, 2 is 3 and 3 is 3 itself. Same for 4 and 5.

In a DSU each set is represented by the leader (or the element with no parent). To find the leader of a set we recursively go to the parent of the current element until we reach an element which is its own parent. Then we return that element. Read the pseudo-code for better understanding 

#### Pseudo-Code
```python
function find(element){
    if (parent[element] == element) 
        return element
    else
        return find(parent[element])
}
```

#### Dry-Run
Let's assume we have a DSU having the following set:
```
     0
   /   \
  1     2
 /
3
```
This will have the following parent array $P$ = [0, 0, 0, 1].  
Here the ${P_i}$ is the parent of index $i$.
If we call find(3), it will run in following steps.
- parent[3] is 1 which is not equal to 3, so we call find(1).
- parent[1] is 0 which is not equal to 1, so we call find(0).
- parent[0] is 0 which equal to 0, so we return 0.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Find in DSU and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Union in DSU
pages.content:
Union operation is used to join two sets into a single set.

We first check if the elements are already in the same set. This can be checked by performing find on both elements and comparing their results. If they have the same leader, we don't have to do anything as they are already in the same set. Otherwise, we set the one set's leader as the parent of another set's leader. Read the pseudo code for better understanding

```python
function union(a, b) {
    leader_a = find(a)
    leader_b = find(b)
    if(leader_a != leader_b){
        parent[leader_b] = leader_a
    }
}
```

#### Dry-Run ####
Let's assume we have a DSU having the following sets:
```
     0
   /   \
  1     2
 /
3
     4
   /   \
  5     6
```
This will have the following parent array $P$ = [0, 0, 0, 1, 4, 4, 4].  
Here the ${P_i}$ is the parent of index $i$.  
If we call union(3, 5), it will run in following steps.
- leader_a will be set to the value returned by find(3) which will be 0.
- leader_b will be set to the value returned by find(5) which will be 4.
- Since leader_a and leader_b are not equal they currently do not belong to the same group.
- So we set parent[leader_a] equal to leader_b
- Thus the new sets will look like this:
```
     0
   / | \
  1  2  4
 /     /  \
3     5    6
```

callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Union in DSU and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.
